title: People copy rule-breaking more than rule-following, and rare overshoots can tip a group
body: On 21 October 2026 psychologists led by Lucas Molleman at the University of Amsterdam reported in [Proceedings of the Royal Society B](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2026.1940) a game played by 750 Americans. A ‘shooting star’ crossed a row of 100 squares; the rule was to click the one that lit up most brightly, but squares further right paid more, and 22.7% of first choices went straight to the best-paying square. After seeing one earlier player’s choice, people barely moved if that player had followed the rule, but moved a long way towards rule-breaking after seeing someone take the top square, more so when that player shared their political party. In 4.4% of cases people went beyond a small violation they had seen, and in the team’s simulations such rare overshoots ratchet a whole group towards rule-breaking, while people who always follow the rule, about a quarter of players, hold it back. Stephen Reicher, a psychologist at the University of St Andrews, [told the Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026/oct/21/bad-apples-rule-breaking-study) that with no penalty for breaking the rule, its real-world relevance is unproven.

slides.question: In a 2026 game the rule was to click the square that lit up most. What share of first choices took the best-paying one?
slides.explanation: 22.7%: before seeing anyone else, almost a quarter of choices broke the rule outright. On average, first choices sat a third of the way from the rule to the top-paying square.

slides.alt: Animation on dark plum: a row of 100 squares lit by a shooting star, with the rule square in blue and pay rising to the right; bars of how far choices moved after seeing others; then a crate of 100 apples ripening from green to red in a simulated group, with and without overshoots.

slides.prompt: Raise the chance that someone overshoots a worse example. How rare can it be and still push the group above 90% rule-breaking?
slides.takeaway: About 4% is enough in this model: each rare overshoot raises the bar for everyone. The study measured 4.4%. A quarter who always follow the rule, about as many as in the study, hold the group far lower.

slides.note: Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 2026. After seeing the rule followed: 1.3 points the other way.

steps.label: Now and then, they go further

slides.heading: What the game leaves out
slides.text: Breaking the rule cost nothing, players were anonymous, and each saw just one other choice; the long run comes from simulations. Stephen Reicher, a psychologist at the University of St Andrews, notes that whom we follow depends on who the others are: many people who see rioting help clear up afterwards.

slides.question: In the 2026 rule-breaking game, which earlier player’s choice moved people’s second choices the most?
options: One who took the top-paying square
One who bent the rule a little
slides.explanation: Seeing someone take the best-paying square moved second choices about 15 points towards rule-breaking, more if that player shared their party. Seeing the rule followed moved them about 1 point back.
